src/benchmark/baseline.py.doc:
FROZEN baseline strategy. Do not edit: any change creates a different benchmark.

This module is deliberately self-contained: it imports nothing from the ranking engine,
strategy selector or UI, so training, tuning or changing CineRankX cannot alter it.
It has no learnable parameters beyond counting the benchmark's training ratings.

  recommend : non-personalised "most popular" -- movies ranked by number of TRAIN
              ratings (ties broken by movieId), minus what the user has already seen.
  predict   : item mean rating, shrunk toward the global mean with a fixed damping.

run_benchmark.py records a SHA-256 of this file next to the baseline's results and
refuses to continue if either the code or the measured numbers differ from the record.

src/benchmark/cinerankx.py.doc:
CineRankX as a benchmark strategy: EASE relevance -> six-objective re-ranking.

Everything here is trained and tuned on the benchmark's TRAIN and VALIDATION splits
only. The frozen baseline never imports this module.

methods.doc: weights=True -> tuned weights for the cohort; None -> plain relevance order (no re-rank).

src/benchmark/metrics.py.doc:
Ranking and rating-prediction metrics for the frozen benchmark.

"Accuracy" in the dashboard is Hit Rate@K: the share of evaluated users for whom at
least one of the top-K recommendations is a held-out movie they rated >= the positive
threshold (4.0). It is stricter than it sounds (a user needs a hit among ~27,000
titles) and saturates for heavy users, which is why Precision, Recall, NDCG and MAP
are always reported next to it.

functions.name: ndcg
functions.doc: Binary-relevance NDCG@K with the ideal ranking limited to min(K, |relevant|) hits.

functions.name: summarize
functions.doc: Mean metrics over users; every list is scored against the same positives.

src/benchmark/split.py.doc:
Frozen benchmark: deterministic train/validation/test split and fixed evaluation cohorts.

Every rating is assigned to a split by a hash of (userId, movieId, seed), so the split
is reproducible without stored state and independent of file order or sample size. The
test interactions are the ground truth for BOTH the frozen baseline and CineRankX;
neither training nor tuning ever reads them.

functions.doc: Pick the EASE regularisation and per-cohort popularity blend by validation NDCG@10.

functions.doc: Objective weights: maximise validation NDCG@10 while staying at least as diverse as the baseline.

the report never has to re-derive numbers the classifier already produced.

imports it, so importing the classifier back would be a cycle.

src/evaluation/recommendation_metrics.py.doc:
Recommendation KPIs, driven off Module 4's final ranked output.

Ground truth is a held-out split of each user's own ratings: the ranker sees
the user's training ratings, and a recommendation counts as a hit if it appears
among the items that user rated POSITIVELY in the held-out portion. Items the
user rated poorly are not hits — recommending a movie someone disliked is not
a success just because they happened to watch it.

Cold-Start Accuracy uses the documented definition: users with <= 5 ratings,
scored against the popularity baseline's top-K on their held-out ratings.

functions.doc: Fraction of the top-K recommendations the user actually liked.

functions.name: recall_at_k
functions.doc: Fraction of the user's liked held-out items that made the top-K.

functions.name: f1_score_at_k
functions.doc: Harmonic mean of Precision@K and Recall@K.

functions.name: average_precision
functions.doc: Average Precision for one user — the per-user term inside MAP.

functions.name: mean_average_precision
functions.doc: MAP: Average Precision averaged over users.

functions.doc: Diversity: mean pairwise genre dissimilarity within one list.

functions.name: novelty
functions.doc: Novelty: mean self-information of the recommended items.

functions.doc: Per-user random hold-out split.

functions.doc: Top-K most-rated movies in the training data — the cold-start reference.

functions.name: evaluate_cold_start
functions.doc: Cold-Start Accuracy: hit-rate for users with <= `max_history` ratings.

functions.name: evaluate_recommendations
functions.doc: Run Module 4 for each user and compute the recommendation KPI group.

src/evaluation/report.py.doc:
Assembles and renders the full KPI report.

Every value is keyed by the exact metric-name string from eval_config.yaml, and
`build_report()` refuses to return a report that is missing a configured KPI —
so a metric cannot silently drop out of the final results table.

functions.name: build_report
functions.doc: Collect the four KPI groups into one report keyed by exact metric names.

functions.name: render

src/evaluation/search_metrics.py.doc:
Search KPIs — Precision@10, Recall@10, MRR, NDCG, Search Latency.

RELEVANCE IS A PROXY, NOT GROUND TRUTH
--------------------------------------
This project has no hand-labeled relevance judgements. Every number in this
module rests on the documented substitute:

    a search result is RELEVANT if it shares at least one genre or keyword
    with the query.

That is a lenient, recall-oriented definition. Two consequences are stated
wherever these metrics are reported rather than buried here:

1. The relevant pool is enormous. A one-word genre query like "action" marks
   thousands of the ~26.7k catalog movies relevant, so **Recall@10 is bounded
   above by 10/|relevant| and is structurally near zero** — it measures the
   catalog's breadth, not the engine's quality. `relevant_pool_size` is
   reported alongside it so the figure stays interpretable.
2. Precision@10 is correspondingly generous: matching one genre is a low bar,
   so a high score here does not imply the results are *good*, only on-topic.

functions.name: _tokenize
functions.doc: Split a genre/keyword cell into a lowercase token set.

functions.name: build_relevance_index
functions.doc: Map movieId -> its genre+keyword token set, for proxy relevance.

functions.name: is_relevant
functions.doc: Apply the documented proxy to one result.

functions.name: precision_at_k
functions.doc: Precision@K: fraction of the top-K results that are relevant.

functions.name: recall_at_k
functions.doc: Recall@K: fraction of ALL relevant items that appear in the top-K.

functions.name: reciprocal_rank
functions.doc: 1 / rank of the first relevant result; 0.0 if none are relevant.

functions.name: ndcg_at_k
functions.doc: NDCG@K with binary gains.

functions.name: evaluate_search
functions.doc: Run every query through the IR engine and compute the search KPI group.

src/evaluation/system_metrics.py.doc:
System KPIs — Response Time, Memory Usage, CPU Usage, Throughput.

Deliberately generic: `measure()` instruments any callable rather than
importing the engines. That keeps this module free of a dependency cycle
(strategy_selector imports src.evaluation.ml_metrics, so src.evaluation must
not import strategy_selector back) and lets the report instrument IR search,
strategy prediction and ranking through one code path.

src/ingestion/build_dataset.py.doc:
CLI entrypoint: loads raw MovieLens + TMDB data, joins them, cleans text,

src/ingestion/joiner.py.doc:
Joins MovieLens movies to TMDB metadata via links.csv, and builds the
per-movie raw text chunk (overview + genres + keywords) used by the IR
engine (Module 2).

TMDB 930K has no cast/crew data (no credits file, no cast/crew columns), so
text_chunk is overview + genres + keywords only — a deliberate scope decision,
not a placeholder. Its genres/keywords are plain comma-separated strings
(unlike TMDB 5000's JSON list-of-dicts), so extraction is a simple split.

Loaders for the raw MovieLens 20M and TMDB 930K CSVs.

names for this dataset pair). MovieLens 20M's genome_scores.csv and
genome_tags.csv are intentionally not loaded here — unused by this pipeline.

src/ranking_engine/__init__.py.doc: Multi-Objective Hybrid Ranking Engine: six weighted objectives.

src/ranking_engine/candidates.py.doc:
Candidate generation: blends Module 2 (IR) and Module 3 (strategy) output.

Module 3's documented guidance (DATASET_MIGRATION.md) is that the predicted
strategy should be treated as a *weighted prior*, not a hard routing decision,
and should degrade toward `collaborative` when classifier confidence is low.
That is implemented here: every candidate source always contributes, and the
predicted strategy only shifts how much each one contributes.

classes.name: CandidateGenerator
classes.doc: Builds a per-user candidate pool from all three strategy sources.

methods.name: _content_candidates
methods.doc: IR engine (Module 2) similarity to the user's best-loved movies.

methods.name: _collaborative_candidates
methods.doc: User-user KNN over the bounded user-item matrix.

methods.name: candidates_for_seed
methods.doc: Gated IR neighbours of one movie, as a ready-to-rank candidate pool.

methods.name: generate
methods.doc: Produce a blended candidate pool for one user.

functions.name: strategy_source_weights
functions.doc: Blend the fallback prior toward the predicted strategy by confidence.

functions.name: genre_overlap_gate
functions.doc: Multiplier in [floor, 1.0] scaling a candidate's IR relevance by genre fit.

functions.name: _normalize
functions.doc: Min-max a source's raw scores into [0, 1] so sources are comparable.

src/ranking_engine/config.py.doc:
Tunable weights for the six ranking objectives.

Weights are read from eval_config.yaml (`ranking_objectives.weights`) and are
never hardcoded in the ranking logic — the ranker only ever asks this object
for a weight by name, so retuning is a config edit, not a code edit.

classes.name: RankingWeights
classes.doc: Weights for the six objectives, normalized to sum to 1.0.

methods.name: items
methods.doc: Iterate objectives in canonical OBJECTIVES order, not dict order.

methods.name: with_overrides
methods.doc: Return a new RankingWeights with some weights replaced.

methods.name: from_config
methods.doc: Load weights from eval_config.yaml's ranking_objectives.weights block.

functions.name: load_genre_gate_floor
functions.doc: Read ranking_objectives.genre_relevance_gate.floor from eval_config.yaml.

src/ranking_engine/ease.py.doc:
EASE item-item linear model: CineRankX's personalised relevance source.

EASE (Steck, 2019) is closed-form ridge regression of every item on all the others,
fit on the binary user-item matrix X of the TRAINING interactions:

    P = (X'X + lambda I)^-1,   B = -P / diag(P),   diag(B) = 0,   score(u) = x_u B

It is classical and explainable (a weighted item-to-item similarity), trains in seconds
on the 6,000 most-rated movies, and scores any user from their own ratings by fold-in --
including a cold-start user with five ratings. Scores are turned into per-user percentile
ranks and blended with a popularity percentile; the blend weight (beta) is tuned on the
validation split, and the multi-objective ranker still produces the final list.

methods.name: fit
methods.doc: Fit on a ratings frame [userId, movieId, rating]; every rating is an interaction.

methods.name: blended_scores
methods.doc: (users x items) = (1-beta) * popularity percentile + beta * per-user EASE percentile.

src/ranking_engine/objectives.py.doc:
The six ranking objectives, plus the catalog statistics they read from.

Two of the six — diversity and coverage — are *set-dependent*: their value for
a candidate depends on which items have already been selected, so they cannot
be precomputed per item. That is why the ranker selects greedily (see
ranker.py) instead of scoring everything once and sorting. The other four are
per-item and are precomputed here.

classes.name: CatalogStats
classes.doc: Per-item statistics for the item-independent objectives, built once.

methods.name: _build_popularity_quality
methods.doc: Bayesian-weighted rating, min-max scaled to [0, 1].

methods.name: _build_novelty
methods.doc: Self-information -log2(p(item)), min-max scaled to [0, 1].

methods.name: popularity_quality
methods.doc: Objective 5: quality weighted by how many people actually voted.

methods.name: novelty
methods.doc: Objective 3: how far off the beaten path this item is.

functions.name: _clean_genre
functions.doc: Strip list/quote punctuation off one genre token and lowercase it.

functions.name: _minmax
functions.doc: Scale to [0, 1]. A constant array maps to all-zeros (no discrimination).

functions.name: diversity_score
functions.doc: Objective 2: how unlike the already-selected items this candidate is.

functions.name: coverage_score
functions.doc: Objective 4: how much of the catalog's genre space this item opens up.

src/ranking_engine/predictor.py.doc:
Baseline rating predictor — the source for the predicted_rating objective.

Uses the classical bias baseline r_hat(u,i) = mu + b_u + b_i with damped
biases. It is deliberately the simplest defensible predictor: the project is
scoped to explainable classical methods, and this model has the property that
matters most for ranking — it degrades gracefully. An unknown user falls back
to mu + b_i (the item's own standing), and an unknown item to mu + b_u, so
cold-start candidates still receive a sensible score instead of a hole.

classes.name: BaselinePredictor
classes.doc: Predicts a user's rating for an item from global/user/item biases.

methods.name: fit
methods.doc: Fit global mean and damped user/item biases from a ratings frame.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Predicted rating on the original rating scale, clipped to [0.5, 5.0].

methods.name: predict_normalized
methods.doc: Objective 6: the predicted rating rescaled to [0, 1].

src/ranking_engine/ranker.py.doc:
Multi-Objective Hybrid Ranking Engine (Module 4).

Re-ranks a blended candidate pool on six weighted objectives. Selection is
*greedy and sequential*, not score-then-sort: diversity and coverage are
defined relative to what has already been chosen, so an item's score is not
fixed until the items above it are. At each step every remaining candidate is
rescored against the current selection and the best-scoring one is taken.

classes.name: MultiObjectiveRanker
classes.doc: Ranks candidates on relevance, diversity, novelty, coverage,

methods.name: _similarity_lookup
methods.doc: Pairwise similarity among candidates, for the diversity objective.

methods.name: rank
methods.doc: Return the top-k re-ranked recommendations for one user.

methods.name: recommend
methods.doc: Convenience wrapper returning just the ranked movieIds.

src/strategy_selector/content_model.py.doc:
Content-based recommender with configurable representation, user profile and quality prior.

Every option is something the held-out experiment can switch independently:
  vectorizer  "base"  TF-IDF over text_chunk_clean, 2,000 terms (the original strategy)
              "rich"  TF-IDF with bigrams, sublinear tf and 20,000 terms
  genre_weight        weight of a genre multi-hot block appended to the (normalised) text vector
  profile     "top20"          rating-weighted sum of the user's 20 best-rated movies (original)
              "liked_centered" weights = rating - user mean over ALL rated movies (dislikes push away)
  quality_alpha       multiplies similarity by (quality percentile) ** alpha: a mild prior towards
                      well-rated, well-voted movies (0 disables it)

functions.name: _quality_percentile
functions.doc: Bayesian-weighted rating percentile (votes shrunk towards the catalog mean).

src/strategy_selector/dataset.py.doc: Build (and cache) the labelled training frame: sampled users -> features + backtest scores.

functions.name: sample_user_ids
functions.doc: Random users with enough (but not extreme) history, from the indexed user_stats table.

functions.name: load_ratings
functions.doc: Ratings of the sampled users, restricted to catalog movies (the strategies' universe).

functions.name: build_labelled_frame

functions.name: make
functions.doc: Unfitted estimator (picklable: classes + keyword arguments only).

src/strategy_selector/formulations.py.doc:
Five ways to turn user features into a strategy choice, behind one sklearn-style interface.

Classes are encoded alphabetically (0 collaborative, 1 content_based, 2 popularity) to match
StrategyClassifier's label encoder; popularity wins score ties, exactly as the labeller does.
Every formulation exposes fit(X, scores), predict_proba(X) (n x 3 strategy preference) and
classes_, so any of them can be saved and used by StrategyClassifier unchanged.

  multiclass   one classifier on the winning strategy
  ovr          one binary "is strategy s the winner?" classifier per strategy
  pairwise     three "a beats b?" classifiers (trained only where a and b differ), summed wins
  regression   predict each strategy's expected hit-rate, choose the highest
  ranking      LambdaRank over the three strategies of each user (strategy-specific features)

classes.name: _Constant
classes.doc: Stand-in for a binary classifier when the training labels contain only one outcome.

classes.name: RankingForm
classes.doc: LambdaRank where each (user, strategy) is a row: user features + strategy id + its inner score.

functions.name: winner
functions.doc: Index of the best strategy per row; popularity (2) wins any tie for first place.

functions.name: _fit_binary
functions.doc: Fit a balanced binary classifier, or a constant when only one outcome occurs.

functions.name: decision_quality
functions.doc: What the choice is worth: realised hit-rate of the chosen strategy vs fixed and oracle policies.

src/strategy_selector/holdout_labeler.py.doc:
Leak-free strategy labels: backtest on a per-user holdout the profile never sees.

Every user's ratings are split once into a PROFILE part and a HOLDOUT part.
Features come from the profile only; every strategy (and the shared popularity
ranking, similarity matrix and TF-IDF profile) is built from profile ratings
only; hit-rates are measured on the holdout. So the ratings that decide a
user's label are invisible to both the features and the strategies.

functions.name: split_profile_holdout
functions.doc: Per-user random split; each user keeps at least one rating on each side.

functions.name: label_holdout
functions.doc: Hit-rate of each strategy on the holdout; raw winner uses the legacy tie-break.

functions.name: clean_labels
functions.doc: Drop users with no clear winner: all-zero scores, or top-two within `margin`.

src/strategy_selector/model_selection.py.doc:
Cross-validated model comparison and one-shot held-out evaluation for the selector.

Rules enforced here: SMOTE only ever sees a training fold (resampling happens
inside each fold, after the split); candidates are ranked by cross-validated
macro-F1 on the development users only; the held-out users are scored once, for
the chosen candidate, and never used to choose anything.

functions.name: build_estimator
functions.doc: Unfitted estimator for a candidate; 'step__param' keys configure pipeline steps.

functions.name: fit_candidate
functions.doc: Fit one candidate on a TRAINING fold (resampling it first when the candidate uses SMOTE).

functions.name: tune_candidate
functions.doc: Randomised search of a candidate's hyperparameters by CV macro-F1 (development users only).

functions.name: _proba
functions.doc: Probabilities aligned to all classes (a fold may have trained without a rare class).

functions.name: cross_validate
functions.doc: Stratified k-fold CV; metrics are per-fold means plus pooled out-of-fold AUC/confusion.

functions.name: compare_candidates
functions.doc: Cross-validate (optionally tuned) candidates on development users; best = top mean macro-F1.

functions.name: evaluate_holdout
functions.doc: Train on all development users, then score the untouched held-out users exactly once.

src/strategy_selector/profile_features.p.doc: Extract user profile features from rating history (vectorized over all users).

functions.doc: (movieId -> genres, movieId -> popularity percentile), built once per catalog object.

functions.name: _popularity_percentile
functions.doc: Catalog popularity percentile per movieId (higher = more popular), if a signal exists.

functions.name: _genre_features
functions.doc: Legacy genre columns plus per-genre affinity (share of a user's ratings in each genre).

functions.name: extract_profile_features
functions.doc: Extract features for each user from their rating history and movie metadata.

src/strategy_selector/stats.py.doc:
Small statistics helpers: bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests.

Users are the unit of resampling (each user contributes one outcome), so intervals reflect
how much a result would move with a different sample of users, not of ratings.

functions.name: bootstrap_ci
functions.doc: (mean, low, high) of the mean of per-user values by percentile bootstrap.

functions.name: paired_bootstrap
functions.doc: Mean of (a - b) over users with a 95% CI and a one-sided bootstrap p-value for 'a is not better'.

functions.name: mcnemar_p
functions.doc: Exact McNemar p-value for 'two classifiers have equal error rates' on the same users.

functions.name: proportion_ci
functions.doc: Wilson interval for an accuracy-style proportion.

src/strategy_selector/strategy_context.p.doc:
Strategy-aware features: a cheap backtest of each strategy on the user's OWN profile.

The label says which strategy won on a hidden holdout. The best available predictor of
that is how the same three strategies score when the user's visible ratings are split
again (profile', pseudo-holdout). These scores, plus popularity-head shares, are computed
by one function used for training and for live prediction, so the two can never drift.
Only ratings passed in are read; the label holdout is never visible.

src/strategy_selector/strategy_labeler.p.doc:
Backtest strategies to determine the best-fit strategy per user.

Performance note: hit-rates are computed against structures built ONCE for
the whole batch (global TF-IDF matrix, a sparse user-item matrix, one
user-user similarity matrix, one popularity ranking) rather than rebuilt from
scratch inside the per-user loop. The original per-user version re-fit a
TfidfVectorizer and rebuilt full rating-vector dicts for up to 500 users on
every iteration, which made it O(users × movies) and timed out past ~1000
users; this version is O(users) after the shared setup.

classes.name: _BacktestContext

functions.doc: Pick the winning strategy from backtested hit-rates.

functions.doc: Build a user's content-based profile vector.

functions.name: label_users_with_best_strategy

src/strategy_selector/utility.py.doc:
Utility-based strategy selection with an uncertainty-aware fallback.

Instead of classifying a noisy "winning strategy" label, predict each strategy's expected
hit-rate (its utility) for the user and pick the best. A non-fallback strategy is only
chosen when its predicted utility beats the fallback's by more than `tau`: small predicted
gaps are within the model's own uncertainty, so the reliable fallback (popularity) is used.

    chosen = argmax_s ( utility_s - tau * [s != fallback] )

tau is a plain, interpretable quantity (hit-rate points) tuned by cross-validation on
development users only. predict_proba is a softmax over the same adjusted utilities, so the
saved model drops straight into StrategyClassifier (argmax == the rule above).

functions.name: choose_tau
functions.doc: Pick the fallback margin that maximises realised hit-rate on out-of-fold utilities.

used for reporting. Writes data/processed/selector_analysis.json.

scripts/build_movielens_only.py.doc:
Build data/processed/ from MovieLens alone (no TMDB), for local demos.

The full pipeline (src.ingestion.build_dataset) needs the TMDB 2023 CSV, which
requires a Kaggle login. This builds the same artifacts from MovieLens 20M only:
overview is empty, keywords come from user tags, and popularity/quality columns
are derived from the ratings themselves.

scripts/compare_smote.py.doc:
Before/after comparison: Module 3's classifier with and without SMOTE.

Both arms share one labeling pass, one feature frame and one train/test split
(train_test_split is seeded at random_state=42 on identical inputs), so the
ONLY difference between them is SMOTE oversampling of the training fold.

scripts/content_experiments.py.doc:
Does a better content representation actually raise held-out hit rate?

Hypothesis: the content-based strategy is weak (hit rate ~0.016) because its representation
(2,000-term TF-IDF, top-20-rated profile, no quality signal) is poor, not because content is
useless. Protocol: the label backtest (70% profile / 30% holdout per user, 30 recommendations);
variants are chosen on a DEVELOPMENT half of users and confirmed on a disjoint half.

Usage: PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/content_experiments.py [n_users]
Writes data/processed/content_experiments.json.

scripts/generate_kpi_report.py.doc:
End-to-end KPI report — the project's final results table.

Computes every metric defined in eval_config.yaml from real data, across all
four engines, and refuses to finish if any configured KPI is missing.

Usage:
    PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/generate_kpi_report.py [n_ratings] [n_users]

Requires the Module 1/2/3 artifacts in data/processed/ (run the ingestion
pipeline and the Module 2/3 verification scripts first).

scripts/label_experiments.py.doc:
Compare label-generation methods: reliability, class mix and what a perfect model could score.

For each configuration the SAME users are labelled twice with independent random holdouts
(seeds 42 and 43). Agreement between the two labelings measures how repeatable a label is;
an oracle ceiling is estimated by simulation (see analyze_selector.noise_ceiling). The
uncertainty-aware variant additionally marks a user "indistinct" when the best strategy does not
beat the runner-up by a one-sided 95% margin (binomial standard error on the holdout size), so
uncertainty is represented instead of being turned into a confident label.

Usage: PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/label_experiments.py [n_users]
Writes data/processed/label_experiments.json.

scripts/run_benchmark.py.doc:
Reproducible strategy comparison: frozen baseline vs. CineRankX on one fixed benchmark.

Usage:
    PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/run_benchmark.py [--refresh-split] [--retune] [--skip-before]

1. Builds (or loads) the frozen split and cohorts from eval_config.yaml `benchmark:`.
2. Scores the FROZEN baseline; compares it with the stored record and aborts on any drift.
3. Tunes CineRankX on the validation split only (or reuses data/benchmark/cinerankx_params.json).
4. Scores the previous CineRankX pipeline ("before") and the improved one ("after") on the
   untouched test split, overall and cold-start, and writes reports/strategy_comparison.json.
5. Retrains the EASE model on all ratings for the live app and saves the tuned blend.

functions.name: before_pipeline
functions.doc: The previous CineRankX pipeline (IR + user-kNN + popularity candidates), unchanged.

functions.name: deploy_winner
functions.doc: Refit the selected candidate on every user, save it for the app, and write the KPI-facing results.

scripts/selector_phase2.py.doc:
Strategy selection, evaluated on TWO separate objectives, with uncertainty and significance.

  Objective A (classification): predict each user's labelled winning strategy.
  Objective B (recommendation value): realised hit-rate of the strategy the selector chooses,
                                       against always-popularity and an oracle.

Protocol: all users kept; stratified 80/20 development/held-out split (seed 42); every model gets the
same 5-fold CV on development users; selection uses CV only; held-out users are scored once per model
for reporting. CIs are user-level bootstraps; significance uses paired bootstraps and McNemar.

Usage: PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/selector_phase2.py [n_users] [--deploy] [--tag NAME]
Writes data/processed/selector_phase2_<tag>.json (tag defaults to the content variant).

classes.name: Reweighted
classes.doc: Wraps a fitted probabilistic model with per-class multipliers (threshold optimisation).

functions.name: tune_thresholds
functions.doc: Per-class probability multipliers that maximise macro-F1 on OUT-OF-FOLD predictions.

scripts/smote_seed_robustness.py.doc:
Multi-seed robustness check for the SMOTE result.

The headline comparison rests on ONE train/test split, where content_based's
true positives moved 5 -> 13 out of 70. Those are small counts, so this script
repeats the identical two-arm comparison across many seeds to separate a real
effect from split luck.

Deliberately standalone: it replicates the classifier's fit path rather than
modifying it, so production code keeps its fixed random_state=42.

functions.name: run_arm
functions.doc: One arm at one seed. Split first; SMOTE only ever sees the train fold.

scripts/smote_vs_class_weight.py.doc:
Does SMOTE do anything that cheaper class_weight tuning does not?

The 10-seed result shows SMOTE lifting content_based RECALL while leaving
ROC-AUC flat. Flat AUC means the probability ranking did not improve — the
model is not discriminating better, it is just pushing the decision boundary
toward the minority class. If that reading is right, simply scaling up the
minority class weights should reproduce the same effect without synthetic
data or an extra dependency. This tests exactly that.

scripts/train_strategy_selector.py.doc:
Train and honestly evaluate the Adaptive Strategy Selector.

Pipeline: sample users (fixed seed) -> per-user profile/holdout split -> features from the
profile only (incl. strategy-aware inner backtest scores) + strategy backtest on the holdout
-> drop ambiguous labels -> hold out 20% of users untouched -> tuned 5-fold CV comparison of
eight model families on the rest (selected by macro-F1) -> one-shot held-out evaluation
-> refit on every labelled user and save model + context.

Usage:
    PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/train_strategy_selector.py [n_users] [--refresh] [--no-tune] [--reliability]

--reliability re-labels the same users with a second independent holdout and reports how often
the two labels agree: the ceiling any classifier can reach on these labels.
Writes data/processed/strategy_eval.json (read by scripts/generate_kpi_report.py).
